title: Oscillations and Waves
lines: This topic links two pictures: one particle vibrating back and forth (oscillation), and a whole pattern of vibration travelling through a medium (a wave). Many exam errors come from mixing up these two pictures, so keep asking which one a question is about. Take g = 10 m/s².
## Simple harmonic motion
- SHM: the restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and directed back towards it: F = −kx, so a = −(k/m)x.
- Amplitude A: largest displacement. Period T: time for one complete oscillation. Frequency f = 1/T. Angular frequency ω = 2π/T.
- Displacement can be written x = A sin(ωt + φ), where φ is the initial phase.
- At equilibrium (x = 0): speed is greatest, acceleration and restoring force are zero. At the extremes (x = ±A): speed is zero, acceleration is greatest.
- In one period a particle travels a distance 4A; in half a period, 2A, wherever it starts. In a quarter period it travels A only if it starts at equilibrium or at an extreme.
> Example: A particle in SHM has x = 0.05 sin(4πt) in metres. Find the amplitude, period and frequency.
> A = 0.05 m. ω = 4π rad/s, so T = 2π/4π = 0.5 s and f = 2 Hz.
! Trap: the acceleration points towards equilibrium, so it is opposite to the displacement, not opposite to the velocity.
## Spring and pendulum periods
- Mass on a spring: T = 2π√(m/k). It does not depend on the amplitude or on g (a vertical spring has the same period as a horizontal one).
- Simple pendulum (small angles, below about 5°): T = 2π√(L/g). It does not depend on the mass or the amplitude.
- With g ≈ π² m/s², a 1 m pendulum has T = 2π√(1/π²) = 2 s.
> Example: A pendulum's length is made 4 times longer. What happens to its period? And a spring-mass system whose mass is made 4 times larger?
> Pendulum: T ∝ √L, so T doubles. Spring: T ∝ √m, so T also doubles.
! Trap: a pendulum clock taken up a mountain (smaller g) has a longer period and runs slow. A spring-mass system would keep the same period.
## Energy in SHM
- Energy changes between kinetic and potential, but the total stays constant (no damping): E = ½kA² = ½mv(max)².
- So v(max) = Aω = A√(k/m). Doubling the amplitude multiplies the energy by 4 and doubles the maximum speed, but leaves the period unchanged.
- Damped oscillation: amplitude and energy decrease; the period stays almost the same.
- Forced oscillation: the system vibrates at the driving frequency. Resonance: the amplitude is greatest when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.
> Example: A 1 kg block on a spring with k = 100 N/m oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Find the total energy and the maximum speed.
## Mechanical waves
- A wave transfers energy and the vibration pattern; the particles of the medium only vibrate about their own positions and do not travel with the wave.

- Transverse wave: particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel (waves on a rope). Longitudinal wave: particles vibrate along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions (sound in air).
- Mechanical waves need a medium. Every particle copies the motion of the source, with a delay.
- Wave equation: v = fλ = λ/T. In one period the wave moves forward one wavelength.
- Frequency is set by the source and stays the same when the wave enters a new medium. Speed is set by the medium. So the wavelength changes in proportion to the speed.
> Example: A sound of 680 Hz travels in air at 340 m/s and then enters water, where sound travels at 1360 m/s. Find the wavelength in each.
> Air: λ = 340/680 = 0.5 m. Water: the frequency stays 680 Hz, so λ = 1360/680 = 2 m.
## Reading wave graphs
- A wave graph (y against position x) is a snapshot of all particles at one instant. The distance between neighbouring crests is λ.
- A vibration graph (y against time t) follows one particle. The time between neighbouring crests is T.

- Direction rule for a wave graph: imagine walking along the graph in the direction the wave travels. A particle on an "uphill" part moves down; a particle on a "downhill" part moves up. Equivalently, each particle will next copy the particle just behind it (closer to the source).
- After a time t, the whole waveform shifts forward by vt. After a whole number of periods the picture looks the same.
> Example: A transverse wave travels in the +x direction with λ = 4 m and v = 2 m/s. Find T, and say how far the waveform shifts in 0.5 s.
> T = λ/v = 2 s. In 0.5 s (a quarter period) the waveform shifts 2 × 0.5 = 1 m, a quarter wavelength, in the +x direction.
> Example: On the same snapshot, a particle sits on a part of the curve rising from a trough to the next crest (moving in +x). Which way does it move now?
> Walking in +x, this part is uphill, so the particle is moving downward.
! Trap: the x-axis of a wave graph is position, not time. Read λ from a wave graph and T from a vibration graph; do not swap them.
## Reflection, superposition and interference
- Waves reflect at a boundary with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence. Echoes are reflected sound.
- Superposition: where two waves meet, the displacements add; afterwards each wave continues unchanged.
- Two sources with the same frequency and a steady phase difference (coherent) produce a stable interference pattern.
- For sources in phase: path difference = nλ gives constructive interference (strong vibration); path difference = (n + ½)λ gives destructive interference (weak or no vibration).
- Diffraction (spreading around obstacles or through gaps) is noticeable when the gap or obstacle is about the same size as the wavelength or smaller.
> Example: Two in-phase sources emit waves with λ = 2 m. A point is 3 m from one source and 4 m from the other. Is it a point of strong or weak vibration?
> Path difference = 1 m = λ/2, so the waves cancel: weak (destructive) vibration.
! Trap: at a point of constructive interference the particle still oscillates; its displacement is not always at maximum, only its amplitude is.
## Standing waves
- Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions form a standing wave with fixed nodes (no vibration) and antinodes (largest vibration).
- Neighbouring nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and the nearest antinode are λ/4 apart. A standing wave carries no energy along the string.
- A string fixed at both ends has nodes at both ends: L = nλ/2, so f = nv/(2L), with n = 1 the fundamental.
> Example: A 0.6 m string carries waves at 120 m/s. Find the fundamental frequency.
> λ = 2L = 1.2 m, so f = 120/1.2 = 100 Hz. The next harmonics are 200 Hz and 300 Hz.
## Sound and the Doppler effect
- Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave; it cannot travel through a vacuum. It is faster in solids than in liquids, and faster in liquids than in gases. In air it is about 340 m/s.
- Pitch depends on frequency; loudness on amplitude. Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; above is ultrasound, below is infrasound.
- Doppler effect: when source and observer approach each other, the observed frequency is higher than the emitted one; when they separate, it is lower. The source's own frequency does not change.
> Example: A student shouts towards a cliff and hears the echo 2 s later. How far away is the cliff (sound at 340 m/s)?
> The sound travels there and back: 2d = 340 × 2, so d = 340 m.
! Trap: as an ambulance passes you, the pitch you hear drops suddenly. That does not mean its siren changed; only the received frequency changed.
## Exam checklist
- Pendulum: T depends on L and g only. Spring: T depends on m and k only.
- Frequency never changes across a boundary; speed and wavelength do.
- For direction questions, use the uphill-down, downhill-up rule in the direction of travel.
